plan.title: Larkspur Self Storage Has Five Night-Shift Rules. I Broke None.
plan.characters: Maya Ortiz (narrator, 24): broke and desperate, takes the night attendant job at Larkspur and tells the story afterward. Walt Brenner (60s): the soft-spoken outgoing attendant who trains her and hands over a laminated rule card. Mr. Ames: a courteous old man in a long, damp-smelling coat who arrives at 2:40 a.m. to 'visit' Unit 114, which no one is allowed to open.
plan.setting: Larkspur Self Storage, a three-floor converted county laundry building off Route 9. It has 212 units, a front desk with a bank of camera monitors, a buzzer gate that locks at midnight, a sign-in ledger dating back to 1961, and a hallway of steel roll-up doors that echo.

parts.events: Maya answers a flyer for a $31-an-hour night job and meets Walt at 9:30 p.m. He gives her a laminated card of five rules: 1) The gate locks at midnight and opens only for Mr. Ames. 2) Never say your own name aloud after midnight. 3) If you hear knocking, knock back the exact same number of times, never more. 4) Mr. Ames may visit Unit 114 at 2:40; never open 114 yourself. 5) If you see yourself on Camera 6, look away until it's gone. Walt leaves at 10 p.m. without eye contact. At 1:13 a.m. three slow knocks come from the third-floor hallway, and she knocks back three on the desk. At 2:15 Camera 6, an empty corridor, shows a person at her desk seen from behind, in her exact gray hoodie.
parts.cliffhanger: She looks away as the rule says, but the figure on Camera 6 lifts a hand and knocks three times. Three knocks answer from underneath her real desk.

parts.events: Shaking, Maya keeps her eyes on the wall until the screen shows only the corridor again. At 2:38 the gate buzzer sounds and the gate swings open before she touches the button. Mr. Ames walks in smelling of wet wool, though the pavement outside is dry. He is gentle and old-fashioned, and he takes the key to 114 from its hook. He asks her name, 'so I can thank you properly,' and she nearly answers before she remembers rule 2 and says only 'the night attendant.' His smile tightens. He mentions that Walt is always generous with new people. He goes down the hall, and the footsteps stop at 114 and do not come back for eleven minutes. She is told never to look, so she stares at the carpet. When he leaves, she opens the old ledger to log his visit.
parts.cliffhanger: Tonight's page already has a line in Walt's handwriting, dated 10:01 p.m., before the shift began: 'Unit 212 — reserved for M. Ortiz.' The building only has 211 numbered doors.

parts.events: Maya takes the master key ring and walks the building with her phone light, breaking no rule. She finds that the ledger lists a different attendant name for each unit from 1 to 211, each with a year, and the dates run from 1961 up to 2002. The staff photo on the break-room wall shows Walt with five coworkers in 2002, and none of those names appear anywhere after that year. Walt's own entry is missing from the ledger. At 3:52 the knocking returns, not three but dozens at once, from every floor, all of it getting louder. She knocks back three on a steel door, and the whole building answers her with one hard knock. She follows the sound down the corridor to the end of the first floor, where a new rolling door stands slightly open. A paper slip on it reads '212 — M. Ortiz.'
parts.cliffhanger: From inside Unit 212, in the dark, three knocks sound from the other side of the open door, and a voice that sounds just like hers whispers, 'You can come in. Walt did.'

parts.events: Maya goes in against her better judgment, because rule 4 only forbids 114. Unit 212 holds a cot, a folding desk, a lamp, and a laminated card identical to hers. Taped inside the lid of a metal box is a torn strip of paper, the missing sixth rule: 'The outgoing keeper is released the moment the incoming keeper's name is spoken aloud inside this building after midnight, by anyone.' Beneath it is a list in Walt's hand of five attendants' names with check marks, and a sixth line that reads 'Maya.' She understands that the knocking is the previous attendants, and that Walt has been bound here for twenty-two years because no replacement ever lasted without speaking their own name. Walt's plan is simply to get someone, anyone, to say hers. She finds her phone's call log shows Walt calling her at 3:20 a.m. She never heard it ring. At 5:40 a.m. the intercom crackles.
parts.cliffhanger: Walt's voice, warm and tired, comes from the gate: 'Maya, shift's almost over. Come open up and tell me your full name so I can sign you out.' Behind her, a wet coat brushes her shoulder, and Mr. Ames says, 'Don't.'

parts.events: Ames tells her the truth in the hallway. He was the first keeper in 1961 and said his own name after midnight, and the building has been calling him by it ever since. It took him, and now he collects what the building takes. He explains the rule system. Every name spoken after midnight is kept, and every keeper who has given theirs is now a knock in the wall, answering to be counted. He says Walt traded names with the building for twenty-two years, feeding it new hires' names to stay alive, and that Walt only wanted to be freed. Maya understands that rule 3 keeps the knockers calm and rule 2 keeps her unclaimed, and that Walt needs her name said so he can walk out. Ames offers her a trade: say any other name aloud and the building takes that one instead. At 5:58 Walt stands at the gate, and she walks to the intercom with the key ring in hand.
parts.cliffhanger: She presses the button and says clearly, 'Walter Brenner, shift's over.' The knocks stop and the gate lock clicks open. Walt's voice vanishes mid-word, and Ames bows, puts his hat on the desk, and dissolves into the first light as the building keeps its name. She walks out at 6:00 a.m. feeling free, then checks her pay stub in the lot: it says 'Maya Ortiz, Night Attendant, hired 2002.' Her car is not there. The gate has locked behind her. It is 9:30 p.m. and a nervous young man with a flyer is standing at the desk, and she hears herself say, 'Welcome to Larkspur. Rule one: never say your name. Rule two: never trust the person who trains you.'

plan.reveal: Larkspur's night rules are the terms of an old bargain with the building itself. Every name spoken aloud after midnight is kept, and the person who spoke it becomes a knock in the walls. Arthur Ames, the first keeper in 1961, was the first name taken, and he now serves as the building's rent collector, appearing at 2:40 a.m. to see whether the new keeper has paid. The units hold the lost attendants, and the knocking is each one answering to be counted, which is why you knock back exactly the same number. Walt Brenner has been bound to the job since 2002, and the only way out is the torn sixth rule: the outgoing keeper is released when the incoming keeper's name is spoken inside after midnight. Walt's whole training was a setup. His rules were real, but he only wanted her kept intact until he could get her name said. Maya saves herself by speaking his name instead, which the building accepts as payment, and Ames is freed in the process. But the building never lets a keeper go. It rewrites her history so she has always worked there, and she takes Walt's place at the desk as the next trainer.

last_narration: Then three knocks answered from underneath my real desk.
